Below is a complete, consolidated 12‑week programme you can use with this 58‑year‑old male client (6 months post‑MI). It integrates the cardiac safety limits you specified (moderate intensity only unless cardiology gives further written clearance), a stronger resistance focus including carefully‑progressed compound lifts (squats and deadlifts with conservative modifications), higher aerobic volume for weight loss, and a supervised 5K time trial at the end. Read and follow the safety rules at the top before starting.

Safety preconditions (read first)
- Obtain written cardiologist clearance: confirm he can perform increased aerobic volume, barbell compound lifts (squats & deadlifts) in submaximal loads, and a supervised 5K test. If cardiologist limits HR or exercise type further, follow medical guidance.
- HR cap for programming: ≲70% age‑predicted HRmax (~115 bpm). If on beta‑blockers or other HR‑blunting meds, rely on RPE (target 11–13 Borg 6–20 scale) rather than HR. Do not exceed RPE 14 without explicit clearance.
- No Valsalva / no maximal lifts / no 1‑RM testing. Teach breathing: exhale on exertion, never hold breath.
- Always screen pre-session for chest pain, new SOB, palpitations, dizziness. Stop and seek medical attention for warning signs.
- Continuous or frequent HR monitoring during sessions (chest strap preferred) and ADAPT loads/rests to maintain HR within limits.
- Supervise all barbell sessions and the 5K time trial; have emergency plan and AED access.

Program overview
- Frequency: 4 gym days/week (2 strength days with compound focus, 2 cardio/conditioning days), plus 1–2 optional low‑intensity active days (walks/mobility). Strength twice/week preserves lean mass; cardio volume increased to support weight loss and 5K prep.
- Structure per session: Warm up (8–12 min) → Main work (25–50 min) → Cooldown & breathing/mobility (8–12 min).
- Progression phases: Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4) — technical foundation + base cardio; Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8) — increase strength stimulus & aerobic volume; Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12) — consolidate strength, add specificity for 5K and optional low‑volume HIIT only if cardiology clears.
- 5K supervised time trial scheduled in Week 12 (tapered build to that event).
- Keep a session log: exercises, sets/reps/weight, HR pre/mid/post sets, RPE, and any symptoms.

Weekly template (applies across phases with progressive overload)
- Monday: Strength Day 1 — Lower compound focus (squat emphasis)
- Tuesday: Cardio Interval Session (moderate intervals; HR ≤ cap)
- Wednesday: Strength Day 2 — Posterior / Full body (deadlift emphasis)
- Thursday: Steady Moderate Cardio (longer continuous session)
- Friday: Optional active recovery or easy cardio / mobility
- Saturday: Long steady aerobic session or mixed cardio (builds base and weight‑loss calories)
- Sunday: Rest / mobility / breathing practice

Progression principles
- Strength: 2‑for‑2 rule conservatively; increase load by ~5% for upper body and 5–10% for lower body if client can do 2 extra reps beyond target on final set for two consecutive sessions without form break and HR remains safe.
- For compounds: remain submaximal — generally target 40–75% of conservative estimated 1RM across the plan; in later weeks you may work in the 60–70% range only if cardiologist approves.
- Aerobic: increase weekly minutes progressively from ~150 min in early weeks toward 200–225 min/week as tolerated and medically cleared.
- Use RPE 11–13 majority of sessions — occasional short sessions up to RPE 13–14 only with clearance.

Detailed week‑by‑week summary (sessions listed with exercises, sets/reps, tempo, rests, HR/RPE notes)

Phase 1 — Weeks 1–4: Foundation, technique, base aerobic
Goal: build movement quality, safety with barbell progression, and base cardio.

Week 1 (example)
Mon — Strength Day 1 (Lower — tech)
- Warm up 10 min: easy bike/walk + dynamic mobility + breathing drills.
- Activation: Hip hinge drills, banded glute bridges 2 x 10, air squats 2 x 10.
- Goblet squat to box: 3 x 10–12, tempo 3‑0‑2, rest 90–120s. Focus form & breathing.
- Trap bar Romanian deadlift (light): 3 x 10–12, rest 90–120s.
- Bulgarian split squat (assisted): 2 x 8–10 each leg, rest 60–90s.
- Pallof press: 2 x 10 each side.
- Cooldown 8–10 min: walk to drop HR + static stretches.

Tue — Cardio Intervals (moderate)
- Warm up 8–10 min.
- 4 x 3 min brisk (work) / 3 min easy recover. Keep HR ≤115 and RPE 11–12.
- Cooldown 8–10 min.

Wed — Strength Day 2 (Posterior/full)
- Warm up 10 min.
- DB Romanian deadlift: 3 x 10–12, rest 90–120s.
- Seated row (machine): 3 x 10–12, rest 60–90s.
- Light empty‑barbell RDL technique practice: 2 x 8 (very light; teach hip hinge).
- Farmer carry: 2 x 30–40s walk.
- Core: Dead bug 2 x 10 each.
- Cooldown 8–10 min.

Thu — Steady cardio
- 30–35 min steady incline walk or recumbent bike at moderate effort (HR ≤115), RPE 11–12.
- Mobility & breathing 8–10 min.

Fri — Active recovery

Considerations before adding HIIT

- Medications: beta‑blockers and some other cardiac drugs blunt heart rate and perceived exertion. If he’s on these, HR is unreliable and RPE must guide intensity. The cardiologist should confirm whether the meds allow safe higher‑intensity exertion.
- Risk vs benefit: HIIT can improve cardiorespiratory fitness and aid weight loss faster than moderate continuous training in many people, but it transiently increases cardiac workload, sympathetic stress, and arrhythmia risk — so it’s higher risk in post‑MI patients unless cleared and carefully supervised.

If cardiology clears HIIT, how to introduce it safely (recommended pathway)
1) Formal clearance:
   - Obtain written clearance specifying acceptable intensity (e.g., target % of peak HR, RPE limits) and any contra‑indications (arrhythmia history, ischemia on exertion tests, uncontrolled BP, heart failure).
   - If available, perform a supervised graded exercise test (GXT) or cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) to determine peak HR, ischemic threshold, and safe exercise intensities.

2) Start very conservatively: "moderate‑intensity intervals" first
   - Before true HIIT, progress with longer moderate intervals at upper end of his cleared zone (e.g., 3–5 min at 60–70% HRmax with equal or longer recovery). This builds tolerance and allows monitoring of HR and symptoms.
   - Use RPE (target 12–13) and ensure HR does not exceed cardiologist limit during these sessions.

3) If cleared for HIIT, use a phased, supervised approach
   - Supervision: sessions should be supervised by you (trainer) and ideally occur where quick medical assistance is available for the first 4–8 sessions.
   - Modality: choose low‑impact modalities (recumbent bike, elliptical, rowing, pool) rather than treadmill sprints to reduce fall/orthostatic risk.
   - Protocol: start with low‑volume, low‑intensity HIIT and progress slowly. Example safe initial HIIT-like protocol (post‑clearance):
     - Warm‑up: 10–15 min easy pedaling/walking, mobility, breathing.
     - Work intervals: 6–8 x 30 seconds at "hard" effort (RPE 13–14) — but ensure HR stays below a cardiologist‑approved limit (may be slightly above prior 70% if explicitly cleared). If HR guidance is unavailable, use RPE 13–14 with close monitoring.
     - Recovery: 90–120 seconds easy pedaling/walking between intervals.
     - Total session time: 20–25 min including warm‑up/cooldown.
   - Progression: gradually increase work interval length (from 30s → 45–60s) and/or number of intervals across weeks, but only if HR and symptoms remain safe and cardiology permits. Aim for total high‑effort time ≤10–15 minutes initially.
   - Frequency: 1 HIIT session/week max initially, with ≥48 hours to full recovery between HIIT sessions. Maintain other sessions as moderate intensity.

4) Safety monitoring during HIIT
   - Continuous HR monitoring (chest strap) and symptom checks before/during/after session.
   - Watch for chest pain, disproportionate breathlessness, dizziness, palpitations, or lightheadedness.
   - Keep resuscitation equipment and emergency plan available when first introducing HIIT (AED location, emergency numbers, cardiologist contact).
   - Stop the session immediately for any warning signs.

Alternative — "Near‑HIIT" or high‑volume moderate intervals (safer)
- If true HIIT is not appropriate, consider "near‑HIIT" or high‑volume moderate intervals: longer intervals at upper end of moderate intensity that do not exceed the HR cap (e.g., 4–5 min work at HR ~65–70% with 3–4 min recovery). - Phase B (next 4 weeks, with clearance): Moderate‑HIIT — 6 x 1 min at RPE 13–14, 2 min recovery; or 8 x 30s at RPE 14 with 90–120s recovery.

- Communicate with the client's cardiologist if you plan to push into higher intensities — provide session plans and monitoring data (HR logs, symptoms).

If cleared, start with low‑volume HIIT on low‑impact equipment, monitor HR and symptoms closely, and limit frequency to once per week initially.
